$comment: Places where official ARO sources disagree with each other, or where an observation differs from a stated rule. status: unresolved = ask the editorial office; reconciled = one action satisfies every source; informational = no action changes because of it.

conflicts.title: Should the submitted manuscript carry author names?

positions.claim: Stage One: put every author's name, affiliation, ORCID and Google Scholar URL on the first page, and do not remove the template's first-page information fields. The editorial office removes all author information after its initial check and before double-blind review.

The Stage-One template has author-name, organisational email, ORCID and Google Scholar fields on its first page, and states that the Editorial Office removes names and affiliations after submission for double-blind review.
Checklist item 7: submit a Word file (.doc or .docx) without author names, following the STAGE-ONE Template.

conflicts.analysis: Two of the three sources, including the template itself and the most detailed page, describe anonymisation done by the editorial office, so authors fill in the first page. The checklist line reads like the generic Open Journal Systems wording that many journals keep by default. It is still an item you tick at submission, so it cannot be ignored. Double-blind review only needs the copy that reviewers see to be anonymous; both readings protect that.
conflicts.recommendation: Email the editorial office (aro.journal@koyauniversity.org) before submitting and ask which version to upload. Prepare both files now: (1) the Stage-One file with every first-page field completed, and (2) an anonymised copy with the author block removed, self-citations written in the third person and the file's author properties cleared. If no reply arrives, follow the Guide and template (completed first page) and say in Comments to the Editor that author details are on page 1 as the Guide to Authors instructs, and that an anonymised copy is attached.

conflicts.title: Abstract: at most 250 words, or 150 to 250?

positions.claim: Under Manuscript Preparation: no more than 250 words.
Under Abstract: between 150 and 250 words, self-contained, without citations.
Checklist item 6: must not exceed 250 words.
No more than 250 words, self-contained, symbols defined, no citations.

conflicts.recommendation: Write 150 to 250 words. That satisfies all four statements.

conflicts.title: Which file format does the first submission need?

positions.claim: Microsoft Word: .doc, .docx or .rtf.
Microsoft Word file (.doc or .docx).
Review stage: online submission in .docx and .pdf.
Required format described as 'Microsoft Word or PDF'.

conflicts.analysis: .docx is accepted by every source. Only the template mentions a PDF alongside it.
conflicts.recommendation: Upload the .docx as the main file. Keep a PDF export ready and include it if the upload screen offers a slot for it, or ask the office together with the anonymisation question.

conflicts.title: AI writing tools: banned, or recommended?

positions.claim: Under Plagiarism: text generated by AI, machine learning or similar algorithmic tools is not allowed, and a violation is scientific misconduct.
Under English Grammar: authors are encouraged to use grammar-check software or ask a native speaker.
A section titled 'Free AI writing tools' lists grammar checkers, paraphrasers and summarisers (Scribbr).

conflicts.analysis: The ban is stated as a misconduct rule; the tool list is a convenience link. The page never says that paraphrasers or summarisers are exempt, and none of the policy pages adds a disclosure route. The only use the Guide clearly endorses is grammar checking.
conflicts.recommendation: Write every sentence yourself. Use spelling and grammar correction only where it fixes your own sentences and does not generate new ones. Do not use paraphrasers, summarisers or chat models to produce, rewrite or translate manuscript text. Keep your drafts and version history as evidence of authorship. Ask the office whether grammar-tool use should be disclosed. Using AI models as the object of your research (for example evaluating or benchmarking them) is a separate matter: describe it fully in Methods.

conflicts.title: Preprint citations: the rule and a published counterexample

positions.claim: Under References: papers available only in preprint repositories (including arXiv) that are not formally peer reviewed may not be cited.
Observed: a 2026 ARO article's reference list includes an item labelled [Preprint].

conflicts.analysis: One published exception does not change a written rule. Reviewers and editors will apply the Guide.
conflicts.recommendation: Follow the rule. Cite the peer-reviewed venue version of every paper (most conference and workshop papers have a published proceedings version). For work that exists only as a technical report on arXiv (many technical reports and model releases), ask the office whether the official model card or repository may be cited as software instead.

conflicts.title: Peer review model wording

positions.claim: Double-blind: author and reviewer identities are kept confidential.
Generic wording: review may be open, transparent or anonymised depending on the journal's policies.
Double-blind peer review.

conflicts.analysis: The ARO-specific pages, the FAQ and the Guide all say double-blind; the policy page uses template wording.

conflicts.title: Author biography: optional or required?

positions.claim: Authors now have the option to include a biography; the corresponding author supplies biographies during registration.
Checklist item 2: provide an academic biography of up to 100 words with a clear statement of affiliation.

conflicts.analysis: The checklist is what you confirm when submitting, so treat it as required.
conflicts.recommendation: Write a biography of at most 100 words for every author, with affiliation stated, and keep it out of the anonymised manuscript copy.

conflicts.title: Issue cut-off dates

positions.claim: Odd issue: papers accepted January to June, closing 30 June. Even issue: July to December, closing 30 December.
Odd issue includes papers accepted by 1 June; even issue by 1 December.

conflicts.analysis: Both pages agree on two issues a year and online-ahead-of-print publication. They differ by a month on the cut-off.
conflicts.recommendation: If you need the paper in a particular issue, plan for acceptance before 1 June or 1 December.

conflicts.title: Impact factor figures differ between pages

positions.claim: Impact factor reported as 2.1 (June 2025).
Web of Science Impact Factor 1.1, Q3 (2025); Scopus CiteScore 3.1 (Q3).

conflicts.analysis: Metrics do not affect submission requirements.
conflicts.recommendation: If a metric matters to you or your institution, check it in Clarivate's Journal Citation Reports rather than quoting either page.

conflicts.title: The template's discipline list has no NLP or AI box

positions.claim: Tick one field that matches your specialty; undeclared disciplines are not considered. Computer Science lists only Software Engineering.
Scope: sciences and engineering, including interdisciplinary work.
Observed: ARO published a natural language processing paper in 2026.

conflicts.analysis: Topics such as NLP have been published in ARO, so they are within scope in practice, but the closest tick box is 'Computer Science: Software Engineering'. 'Undeclared disciplines are not considered' makes the tick box consequential.
conflicts.recommendation: Ask the office which box an NLP / AI paper should tick, in the same email as the anonymisation question. Until then, plan to tick Computer Science.

conflicts.title: Associate Editors are mentioned but not listed

positions.claim: An Associate Editor selects reviewers and recommends acceptance, revision or rejection to the Editor-in-Chief.
The Editorial Team page lists only Executive Editors.

conflicts.analysis: You do not need to know who your handling editor is. It only explains why the directory has no Associate Editor section.

conflicts.title: Stated review times and one observed timeline

positions.claim: Initial review takes about 4 to 6 weeks; a decision typically 8 to 12 weeks from submission.
Observed: one 2026 article was received 2 January, accepted 19 June and published 15 August.

conflicts.analysis: A single example is not a statistic, but it shows that the stated range is a typical case, not a promise.
conflicts.recommendation: Plan for longer than 12 weeks if a deadline (graduation, a course, a grant report) depends on acceptance.
